practices.name: Leadership & Executive Coaching
practices.meta_title: Leadership & Executive Coaching for Growing Companies
practices.meta_description: Executive and team coaching grounded in behavioral science that helps leaders gain clarity, decide well under pressure and build teams that drive growth.
practices.tagline: Coaching that treats leadership as behavior: observable, measurable and capable of real change.
intro: Leadership effectiveness is a behavior, and behavior can be observed, understood and changed. Our leadership and executive coaching practice works with leaders and teams at every level, from founders in fast-growth startups to senior executives in large enterprises. We are especially at home in fast-growing, knowledge-based businesses, where the leader's habits of attention, communication and judgment shape how quickly the whole organization can learn.

Our coaches bring a background in clinical and health psychology, research methods and psychometrics, and many years of founding and building companies. That combination lets us blend research-based insight with practical, real-world coaching. We help leaders gain clarity on what matters, shift the mindsets that keep them stuck, align their teams around shared commitments, and make sound decisions when the stakes are high and the information is incomplete.

Every engagement is tied to outcomes that matter to the business. We agree on the behaviors that will change, how stakeholders will notice, and which signals in engagement, retention, execution or customer data should move as a result. Coaching then follows our engagement method, Observe, Signal, Design, Test and Scale, so that personal growth becomes organizational capability rather than a private conversation that fades.

themes.title: Clarity before action
themes.body: Leaders under growth pressure often act on assumptions they have never examined. We help them separate what they know from what they believe, name the few priorities that truly drive results, and translate those priorities into specific behaviors their teams can see. Clarity is not a feeling; it is a shared, observable agreement about what matters now and what can wait.

themes.title: Teams as engines of growth
themes.body: Most organizational performance lives in teams, not individuals. We coach teams to build explicit charters, healthy conflict, psychological safety and disciplined decision rights. The goal is a team that learns faster than its market changes, holds itself accountable without constant escalation, and multiplies the capability of every leader on it rather than depending on one person's heroics.

themes.title: Measured, not merely felt
themes.body: Coaching should change something others can observe. We define success at the outset using stakeholder input, structured 360 feedback and business signals the organization already tracks. Progress is reviewed against those indicators throughout the engagement, so sponsors see evidence of change and leaders receive honest, specific feedback about what is working and what still needs attention.

practices.name: Health & Behavioral Medicine
practices.meta_title: Health Behavior Change & Behavioral Medicine Consulting
practices.meta_description: Behavioral medicine expertise for health systems, digital health and wellness firms: adherence, engagement, health communication and clinician wellbeing.
practices.tagline: Helping people do the healthy things they already want to do, and measuring whether it works.
intro: Health outcomes depend on behavior. Taking a medication as prescribed, returning for a follow-up visit, logging symptoms in an app, staying with an exercise routine, or a clinician finding the energy to practice well at the end of a long week: each is a behavior shaped by motivation, ability, environment and timing. Our health and behavioral medicine practice applies the science of behavior change to these moments, where good intentions so often fail to become consistent action.

Our approach is grounded in clinical health psychology and behavioral medicine. That grounding informs how we design: with respect for the patient's lived reality, attention to health literacy and access, and the rigor of research methods and measurement.

We work with health systems, digital health companies, payers, employers, health clubs and wellness brands. Using our Observe, Signal, Design, Test and Scale method, we find the behavioral signals that predict engagement and adherence, design interventions grounded in established health behavior models, test them carefully, and help teams sustain what works. Throughout, our standard is ethical persuasion: support for people's own goals, never manipulation.

themes.title: Behavior change grounded in evidence
themes.body: We draw on established frameworks such as COM-B, the Fogg Behavior Model, self-determination theory and motivational interviewing. These models help us diagnose why a healthy behavior is not happening, whether the gap is capability, opportunity, motivation or a missing prompt, and then design interventions that address the actual barrier rather than repeating reminders that people have already learned to ignore.

themes.title: Designing for real patients and members
themes.body: People managing illness are often tired, anxious, juggling costs and decoding unfamiliar language. We design for those conditions: plain-language communication, low-effort first steps, respect for autonomy, and attention to caregivers and family. Experience design and service design make healthy behavior easier, while research with real patients and members keeps assumptions in check before they become expensive programs.

themes.title: Caring for the people who give care
themes.body: Clinicians and care teams are the delivery system for every health intervention. Burnout erodes quality, safety and retention long before it appears in a survey. We apply organizational psychology and behavioral design to workload, workflow and team climate, focusing on the systemic drivers of exhaustion rather than asking already stretched professionals to simply become more resilient.

services.name: Executive Coaching
services.meta_title: Executive Coaching Grounded in Behavioral Science
services.meta_description: Executive coaching that ties leader growth to measurable outcomes, using stakeholder-centered methods, 360 feedback and clear, confidential contracting.
services.summary: One-to-one executive coaching that combines psychology, stakeholder feedback and business signals to change the leadership behaviors that matter most.
services.lede: Our executive coaching helps senior leaders and founders change the specific behaviors that limit their impact, with clear contracting, honest stakeholder feedback and progress measured against outcomes the business already cares about.
challenge: Senior leaders rarely receive candid feedback. The higher they rise, the more people filter what they say, and the more a leader's blind spots are amplified across the organization. Many executives also carry habits that served them well earlier in their careers, such as deep personal involvement in every decision, fast and forceful opinions, or a preference for harmony over conflict, which now quietly slow their teams down. Without a structured way to see these patterns, leaders keep working harder at the wrong things.

Executive coaching itself is often vague. Engagements begin without clear goals, sponsors are unsure what is happening behind closed doors, and success is judged by whether the leader enjoyed the conversations. Confidentiality is poorly defined, so leaders hold back. When the engagement ends, there is little evidence of change and no plan to sustain it. Good executive coaching requires the same discipline as any serious investment: explicit contracting, defined behaviors, credible measurement and a path to lasting habit.

approach.title: Contracting and discovery
approach.body: We begin with a three-way contracting conversation among the leader, the sponsor and the coach, agreeing on goals, roles and what stays confidential. We then interview stakeholders, review relevant context, and where useful administer validated assessments. The aim is a clear, shared picture of how the leader is experienced by others and what the business needs from them next.

approach.title: Focus on few behaviors
approach.body: We synthesize 360 feedback and interview themes into a small number of development priorities, usually one to three observable behaviors. We connect each to signals the organization already tracks, such as team engagement, retention, decision speed or execution against plan, so that change can be noticed by stakeholders and reflected in the data rather than only felt by the leader.

approach.title: A practical coaching plan
approach.body: Together we design a coaching plan built around real situations on the leader's calendar: upcoming board meetings, difficult conversations, hiring decisions or reorganizations. We use behavioral design principles to make new habits easy to start and to attach them to existing routines, and we prepare the leader to enlist stakeholders as allies in noticing progress.

approach.title: Practice and feedback loops
approach.body: The leader tries new behaviors in live settings and we debrief what happened. Following a stakeholder-centered coaching approach, the leader checks in regularly with key colleagues to ask for brief, forward-looking suggestions. Midpoint pulse feedback shows whether others perceive change, so we can adjust the plan rather than waiting until the end to learn what worked.

approach.title: Sustain and extend
approach.body: We close with a final stakeholder review, a comparison against the original goals and a written sustainability plan. Where appropriate, we extend gains to the leader's team through team coaching or alignment sessions, so that better leadership behavior becomes part of how the group operates rather than something that depends on the coach being present.

deliverables: Three-way coaching agreement with confidentiality boundaries
Stakeholder interview synthesis and 360 feedback report
Individual development plan with one to three priorities
Midpoint stakeholder pulse survey and debrief
Final progress review against agreed goals
Written sustainability plan for continued growth
outcomes: Leaders gain a clear, evidence-based view of how colleagues actually experience them
Stakeholders notice specific, sustained changes in the leader's day-to-day behavior
Sponsors see progress against agreed goals without compromising coaching confidentiality
Teams benefit from clearer direction, better delegation and more productive conflict
services.who_we_serve: We coach chief executives, founders, senior vice presidents and high-potential leaders stepping into larger roles. Typical clients lead fast-growing technology and professional services firms, health organizations, financial services companies and associations. Engagements often begin at a trigger moment: a promotion into the executive team, a founder handing operations to a new leadership layer, feedback that a strong performer is creating friction, a merger or reorganization, or a board asking a leader to develop specific capabilities before the next stage of growth.
services.impact_lens: When an executive changes how they listen, decide and delegate, the effect reaches far beyond the leader. Employees experience clearer priorities and more respect for their judgment, which supports engagement and wellbeing. Customers and patients benefit from teams that can focus on their needs instead of navigating internal friction. In mission-driven organizations, better leadership means scarce resources go further for the communities they serve. Coaching that respects autonomy and confidentiality also models the kind of ethical influence we want leaders to practice.

faqs.q: What is executive coaching, and how is it different from therapy or consulting?
faqs.a: Executive coaching is a structured, goal-focused partnership that helps a leader change specific behaviors tied to their role and the organization's needs. Unlike therapy, it does not aim to treat clinical concerns or explore personal history in depth, though our clinical background helps us recognize when a referral is appropriate. Unlike consulting, the coach does not solve the business problem for the leader; the coach builds the leader's capacity to solve it.

faqs.q: How do you handle confidentiality with the sponsoring organization?
faqs.a: Confidentiality is agreed in writing at the start. Typically, the content of coaching conversations stays between the leader and the coach, while goals, the development plan and overall progress are shared with the sponsor in three-way meetings. The leader decides what personal material, if any, is disclosed. Clear boundaries let leaders speak openly and give sponsors enough visibility to support the investment.

faqs.q: How do you measure whether executive coaching worked?
faqs.a: We define success before coaching begins. Stakeholders who work closely with the leader provide input at the start, at the midpoint and at the end, rating perceived change on the specific behaviors chosen. We also look at relevant business signals, such as team engagement or retention, while being careful not to attribute every movement to coaching alone. The combination gives an honest view of progress.

faqs.q: How long does an executive coaching engagement last?
faqs.a: Most engagements run between six and twelve months, which is usually enough time for new behaviors to be practiced, noticed by colleagues and turned into habits. Sessions are typically every two to three weeks, with brief check-ins between them around important events. Shorter, focused engagements are possible for a specific transition, such as preparing for a new role or a major board presentation.

services.name: High-Performance Team Coaching
services.meta_title: High-Performance Team Coaching for Leadership Teams
services.meta_description: Team coaching that turns capable individuals into high-performance teams through charters, psychological safety, clear decision rights and shared goals.
services.summary: Team coaching for leadership and cross-functional teams that builds shared purpose, healthy conflict and accountable execution, measured against real business signals.
services.lede: Our team coaching helps leadership and cross-functional teams become high-performance teams, with explicit charters, psychological safety, clear decision rights and habits of accountability that turn a group of talented individuals into an engine of growth.
challenge: Many teams are teams in name only. Each member is capable and committed, but meetings are status updates, real disagreements surface in hallways afterward, and decisions are revisited because nobody was sure who owned them. In fast-growing organizations the problem compounds: new leaders join faster than norms can form, priorities shift every quarter, and the team spends more energy coordinating than executing. The leader often fills the gaps personally, which becomes a bottleneck as the company scales.

Off-site retreats and personality workshops rarely fix this. They generate goodwill and a shared vocabulary, but the team returns to the same calendar, incentives and habits. Lasting change requires working on the team as a system: its purpose, membership, agreements, decision processes and the everyday behaviors that build or erode trust. Team coaching addresses these directly, in the context of the team's real work, and checks whether the changes hold over time.

approach.title: Diagnose the team system
approach.body: We interview each member, observe the team in its regular meetings and gather perspectives from key stakeholders outside the team. A validated team effectiveness survey adds a structured baseline. We look at purpose, membership, decision rights, conflict patterns and psychological safety, and we pay attention to how the team's work actually flows rather than how the organization chart says it should.

approach.title: Identify the limiting patterns
approach.body: We synthesize what we observed into a small set of patterns that most limit performance, such as unclear ownership, avoided conflict or meetings that do not produce decisions. We link each pattern to business signals the team already watches, from cycle time to cross-functional handoffs to engagement scores, so the team can see why these behaviors matter.

approach.title: Build the team charter
approach.body: In facilitated working sessions the team creates a charter: its shared purpose, the outcomes only this team can deliver, decision rights, meeting cadence and explicit norms for conflict and accountability. We use tools such as decision matrices and pre-mortems so the charter reflects real tradeoffs rather than aspirational statements nobody will remember next month.

approach.title: Coach the team in action
approach.body: We attend selected team meetings and coach in the moment, helping the group practice its new agreements under real pressure. Short retrospectives after key decisions show what is working. A midpoint pulse survey compares current team behavior with the baseline, and the team adjusts its charter where agreements are not holding or no longer fit.

approach.title: Make it self-sustaining
approach.body: We help the team build its own rituals for reflection and renewal, so it no longer needs a coach to stay healthy. We often extend the work to the next layer of leaders, cascading charters and decision rights so that the leadership team's habits shape how the wider organization collaborates and executes.

deliverables: Team effectiveness baseline survey and interview synthesis
Written team charter with purpose and decision rights
Meeting redesign with clear agendas and decision protocols
Pre-mortem and retrospective templates for ongoing use
Midpoint and final team pulse reports
Sustainability plan with rituals for team renewal
outcomes: Team members share a clear understanding of purpose, priorities and who decides what
Disagreements surface in the room and are resolved with less escalation to the leader
Meetings produce decisions and commitments rather than repeated status updates
The team learns and adapts faster as the business and market change
services.who_we_serve: We work with executive teams, founding teams adding their first senior hires, cross-functional product and go-to-market teams, and clinical or operational leadership teams in health organizations. Common triggers include a new chief executive forming a team, rapid headcount growth, a merger that brings two leadership groups together, repeated missed commitments, or engagement data suggesting low trust. Team coaching is also valuable after a successful period, when a team wants to raise its standard before the next phase of growth.
services.impact_lens: Teams are where most people spend their working lives, and team climate shapes whether employees feel respected, safe to speak up and able to do their best work. High-performance teams make better, faster decisions for customers and patients, and they waste less of their organization's resources on rework and politics. For nonprofits and health organizations, a well-functioning leadership team means more of the mission's limited capacity reaches the people and communities it is meant to serve.

faqs.q: What is the difference between team coaching and team building?
faqs.a: Team building usually focuses on relationships and shared experience, often in a single event. Team coaching is a sustained engagement focused on how the team actually works: its purpose, decision rights, meeting practices, conflict norms and accountability. Relationships improve as a result, but the target is performance on real work. Team coaching also includes measurement, so the team can see whether its new agreements are holding.

faqs.q: What goes into a team charter?
faqs.a: A useful team charter answers a few practical questions. Why does this team exist, and what outcomes can only it deliver? Who is on the team, and what is each person accountable for? Which decisions does the team make together, and which belong to individuals? How will we run meetings, handle disagreement and hold each other to commitments? The charter is revisited regularly, not filed away.

faqs.q: How does psychological safety fit into team coaching?
faqs.a: Psychological safety, the shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, is a foundation for learning and candor. We treat it as a set of observable behaviors: how leaders respond to bad news, whether quieter members are invited in, how mistakes are discussed. We coach those behaviors directly while keeping standards high, because safety without accountability tends to become comfort rather than performance.

faqs.q: Can team coaching work alongside individual executive coaching?
faqs.a: Yes, and the combination is often powerful. Individual coaching helps each leader work on personal patterns, while team coaching addresses the dynamics between them. We keep the two clearly separated in terms of confidentiality, so that nothing shared in individual sessions is brought into the team without the leader's consent. Coordinating the two lets individual growth and team agreements reinforce each other.

services.name: Leadership Development Programs
services.meta_title: Leadership Development Programs That Change Behavior
services.meta_description: Leadership development programs designed with behavioral science: cohort learning, coaching and on-the-job practice tied to the behaviors your business needs.
services.summary: Cohort-based leadership development programs that build practical skills through applied projects, peer coaching and measured behavior change on the job.
services.lede: We design and deliver leadership development programs that change what leaders actually do at work, combining cohort learning, individual and peer coaching, applied projects and measurement tied to the behaviors your organization needs most.
challenge: Organizations invest heavily in leadership development programs, yet participants often return to the same pressures and habits a week later. Content is generic, drawn from frameworks that are not connected to the company's strategy or culture. Sessions are scheduled away from real work, so there is little chance to practice. Managers of participants are not involved, and nobody follows up to see whether anything changed. The program is judged by satisfaction scores rather than by what leaders do differently.

Growing companies face an added challenge: they promote strong individual contributors into management quickly, often with little preparation. These new leaders know the work but have never had to delegate, give difficult feedback, run a team meeting or make tradeoffs among competing priorities. Without deliberate development, they either micromanage or withdraw, and their teams feel the effect. Good leadership development programs treat these transitions as predictable behavioral challenges and prepare leaders before problems compound.

approach.title: Define the leadership need
approach.body: We interview senior leaders, current managers and their teams, and review engagement, retention and performance data to understand where leadership behavior is helping or hurting. We clarify which roles and transitions matter most, and what good leadership looks like in this specific organization, not in a generic competency model borrowed from elsewhere.

approach.title: Translate into measurable behaviors
approach.body: We convert the leadership need into a short list of observable behaviors, such as delegating decisions with clear boundaries or holding regular one-to-ones. For each, we define how it will be measured, through 360 items, team pulse surveys or operational signals, establishing a baseline before the program starts so that progress can be assessed honestly.

approach.title: Build the learning journey
approach.body: We design a program that blends short, focused learning sessions with practice on real work. Elements typically include cohort workshops, peer coaching circles, individual coaching, applied projects tied to business priorities and manager involvement. We use behavioral design to make new practices easy to try, with prompts, templates and routines that fit into a leader's normal week.

approach.title: Pilot and refine
approach.body: We run a pilot cohort first, gathering feedback after every session and measuring early behavior change through participant and team surveys. We look for which components actually drive practice on the job and which are merely enjoyable. The program is refined before wider rollout, saving the organization from scaling something that sounds good but does not work.

approach.title: Roll out and build capability
approach.body: We scale the program across cohorts and train internal facilitators and coaches so the organization owns the capability. Dashboards track behavior change over time, and alumni networks keep practices alive. We help leadership connect the program to promotion criteria and performance conversations, so development becomes part of how the organization grows leaders, not a one-time event.

Program architecture with sessions, coaching and projects
Facilitator guides, participant workbooks and practice tools
Pre- and post-program 360 and team pulse measures
Pilot cohort evaluation with recommended refinements
Internal facilitator training and program handoff plan
outcomes: New managers make the transition to leadership with fewer costly missteps
Leaders consistently practice the specific behaviors their teams notice and value
Program investment is evaluated by behavior change, not only satisfaction

services.who_we_serve: We design programs for chief people officers, learning and development leaders and chief executives in growing technology companies, professional services firms, health systems and associations. Typical triggers include rapid promotion of first-time managers, a new leadership competency model that needs to come to life, succession planning for senior roles, engagement data pointing to manager effectiveness, or a private equity owner asking for stronger leadership bench strength across a portfolio company.
services.impact_lens: Managers are the single strongest influence on most employees' daily experience at work. Better leaders mean clearer expectations, fairer feedback and more growth for the people who report to them, which supports wellbeing as well as performance. Customers and patients feel the difference in more consistent service. Programs that develop leaders from diverse backgrounds and new-to-role managers also widen access to leadership opportunity within the organization and the communities it draws talent from.

faqs.q: How are your leadership development programs different from off-the-shelf training?
faqs.a: Off-the-shelf programs teach general concepts. Ours begin with the specific behaviors your organization needs, defined through research with your leaders and teams, and they are measured against a baseline. Most of the learning happens through practice on real work, with coaching and peer support, rather than in a classroom. The content draws on established research, but it is shaped to your strategy and culture.

faqs.q: How long does a typical leadership development program run?
faqs.a: Most cohort programs run from four to nine months. That allows enough time between sessions for participants to practice new behaviors, receive feedback and form habits. Program length depends on the audience: first-time manager programs are often shorter and more practical, while senior leadership programs tend to include more individual coaching and strategic project work.

faqs.q: How do you measure the impact of leadership development?
faqs.a: We measure behavior change rather than only satisfaction. Before the program, participants and their teams complete short surveys on the target behaviors. We repeat them at the midpoint and after the program. Where possible, we also examine related signals such as team engagement, retention or internal promotion rates, while being careful about attributing changes solely to the program.

faqs.q: Can you train our internal team to deliver the program?
faqs.a: Yes. Building internal capability is part of the Scale phase. We train internal facilitators and coaches, provide complete guides and materials, and observe early sessions to offer feedback. Many clients keep us involved for individual coaching of senior participants or for periodic program reviews while their internal team runs the core curriculum.

services.name: Decision-Making Under Pressure
services.meta_title: Decision-Making Under Pressure: Coaching for Leaders
services.meta_description: Coaching and team practices that help leaders make sound decisions under pressure, using pre-mortems, decision rights and research on expert intuition.
services.summary: Coaching and practical tools that improve how leaders and teams make high-stakes decisions when time is short and information is incomplete.
services.lede: We help leaders and teams improve decision-making under pressure by combining research on expert intuition and cognitive bias with practical tools, deliberate practice and coaching on the emotional side of high-stakes choices.
challenge: Leaders in growing organizations make consequential decisions every week with incomplete data, tight timelines and real uncertainty. Under pressure, predictable patterns emerge. Some leaders freeze and seek more information than the situation allows. Others decide too quickly, anchoring on the first plausible option. Stress narrows attention, emotions color risk perception, and teams defer to the most senior or most confident voice in the room. The cost of these patterns rarely shows up immediately, which makes them easy to overlook.

Most advice on decision-making assumes calm, analytical conditions that rarely exist in practice. Research on naturalistic decision-making shows that experienced professionals often decide by recognizing patterns and mentally simulating a course of action, a process described as recognition-primed decision-making. That intuition can be excellent when it has been trained in a stable environment with good feedback, and dangerous when it has not. Leaders need to know which situation they are in, and they need team processes that catch errors before they become costly.

approach.title: Study real decisions
approach.body: We review recent consequential decisions with the leader and team, reconstructing what was known, how options were framed, who was involved and how the choice was made. Interviews and observation of decision meetings reveal patterns: where intuition worked well, where bias crept in, and where unclear decision rights slowed things down or caused rework.

approach.title: Map decision risks
approach.body: We identify the decision types that matter most to the business, and for each we assess time pressure, reversibility, available feedback and the leader's experience. This shows where fast, intuitive judgment is appropriate and where a more structured process is warranted. We also identify early signals that a decision is going off track.

approach.title: Build decision tools and habits
approach.body: We design lightweight tools that fit the pace of the business: decision rights matrices, pre-mortems that imagine failure in advance, red-team roles, explicit criteria agreed before options are debated, and short decision logs. We pair these with individual coaching on managing stress responses, noticing emotional state and slowing down for a moment when it matters.

approach.title: Practice under realistic conditions
approach.body: Leaders and teams rehearse decisions through tabletop scenarios and simulations built from their own context, receiving feedback on both process and outcome. We then apply the tools to live decisions and debrief afterward. Decision logs let leaders compare their predictions with what actually happened, building calibration over time.

approach.title: Embed decision discipline
approach.body: We help the organization embed effective practices into planning cycles, investment reviews and incident response, and we train internal facilitators to run pre-mortems and after-action reviews. The aim is a culture where decisions are made at the right level, at the right speed, and where the organization learns systematically from both good and poor outcomes.

deliverables: Decision audit of recent high-stakes choices
Decision rights matrix for key decision types
Pre-mortem and after-action review facilitation guides
Scenario-based simulation exercises tailored to your context
Decision log template with calibration review process
Individual coaching plan for stress and judgment
outcomes: Leaders match their decision process to the stakes, speed and reversibility involved
Teams surface risks and dissenting views before commitments are made, not after
Decisions are made at the right level, with less escalation and rework
The organization learns systematically from decisions through regular after-action reviews
services.who_we_serve: This work suits chief executives, founders, operating leaders and executive teams who face frequent high-stakes choices: capital allocation, product bets, hiring and restructuring, crisis response and clinical or safety decisions. It is also valuable for investment committees and boards. Common triggers include a costly decision that was made too fast or too slowly, a crisis that exposed unclear authority, rapid growth that pushes more decisions onto new leaders, or a leader who reports feeling overwhelmed by the volume and weight of choices.
services.impact_lens: Decisions made under pressure ripple outward. In health organizations they shape patient safety and care quality. In financial services and lending they affect customers' financial lives. Inside any organization, better decisions mean fewer whiplash reversals, more stable jobs and less stress for employees who must carry out the choices. Leaders who understand the emotional dimension of judgment also make fairer, more humane decisions about the people affected, which builds trust in the organization and the communities it serves.

faqs.q: What is recognition-primed decision-making?
faqs.a: Recognition-primed decision-making is a model from naturalistic decision research describing how experienced professionals decide quickly in real settings. Rather than comparing many options, they recognize a situation as familiar, identify a workable course of action and mentally simulate it to check for problems. It works well when experience was built with reliable feedback. Coaching helps leaders know when their intuition can be trusted and when it cannot.

faqs.q: What is a pre-mortem, and why is it useful?
faqs.a: A pre-mortem asks a team to imagine that a decision has already failed and then explain why. Because it frames dissent as a creative exercise rather than disloyalty, it surfaces risks that people might otherwise keep to themselves. It counters overconfidence and groupthink with minimal time investment. We teach teams to run pre-mortems for significant decisions and to turn the identified risks into specific mitigations.

faqs.q: Can coaching really help with stress during difficult decisions?
faqs.a: Yes. Stress narrows attention and can push leaders toward either rash action or avoidance. Drawing on our background in clinical and health psychology, we help leaders recognize their own stress signals, use brief techniques to regain focus and build routines that protect their judgment, such as sleep, preparation and trusted thinking partners. The goal is not to eliminate pressure but to decide well within it.

faqs.q: Is this service for individuals or teams?
faqs.a: Both. Many decision-making problems are team problems: unclear decision rights, deference to hierarchy or a lack of genuine dissent. We often combine individual coaching for the senior leader with team sessions that build shared decision tools and norms. Some clients start with a decision audit to see where the biggest gaps lie before choosing the right mix.

services.name: Leadership Alignment & Engagement
services.meta_description: Leadership alignment work that turns strategy into shared priorities and visible behaviors, so leaders pull together and employees stay engaged through change.
services.summary: Facilitation, coaching and measurement that align senior leaders on priorities and behaviors, and carry that alignment through to employee engagement.
services.lede: Leadership alignment means senior leaders agree on what matters, act consistently and communicate one story to the organization. We build that alignment through structured dialogue, coaching and measurement, and trace its effects through to employee engagement.
challenge: Strategy documents often look aligned while the leadership team is not. Each executive interprets priorities through the lens of their own function, resources are allocated to protect existing commitments, and mixed messages reach employees within days of a planning offsite. Employees notice when leaders say one thing and fund another, and they respond rationally by waiting, hedging or disengaging. Misalignment is rarely visible in a single meeting, but it shows up clearly in slow execution and declining engagement scores.

Engagement surveys are frequently treated as a human resources exercise, separate from strategy. Results arrive, action plans are written, and little changes because the root causes sit in leadership behavior: unclear priorities, inconsistent decisions, and limited recognition or growth. Improving engagement sustainably requires leadership alignment first. When leaders agree on direction and model consistent behavior, engagement becomes a leading indicator of execution rather than a lagging score to be managed.

approach.title: Surface the real differences
approach.body: We interview each senior leader confidentially about strategy, priorities, tradeoffs and concerns, and speak with a sample of managers and employees about how strategy is experienced on the ground. We review planning documents and engagement data. This reveals where leaders genuinely disagree, where they think they agree but do not, and where messages are getting lost.

approach.title: Find the engagement drivers
approach.body: We analyze engagement and pulse survey data alongside retention and performance signals to identify which drivers actually predict outcomes in this organization. Often a few factors, such as clarity of priorities or confidence in leadership decisions, explain much of the variation. Those become the predictive KPIs for alignment work, rather than an overall engagement index.

approach.title: Agree on priorities and behaviors
approach.body: In facilitated sessions the leadership team confronts the differences we found, makes explicit tradeoffs and agrees on a small set of priorities. They also commit to specific leadership behaviors and a shared narrative for the organization. We design a communication cascade and feedback loops so that alignment reaches managers and frontline teams intact.

approach.title: Check alignment in practice
approach.body: We run short pulse surveys and listening sessions to test whether employees understand the priorities and see leaders acting consistently. Where messages are distorted or behaviors slip, we coach individual leaders and adjust the cascade. Testing early keeps small inconsistencies from growing into widespread skepticism about the strategy.

approach.title: Build an alignment rhythm
approach.body: We help the organization establish a regular operating rhythm: quarterly priority reviews, leadership behavior check-ins and engagement dashboards focused on the drivers that matter. Managers receive tools to discuss priorities with their teams. Alignment becomes a continuing leadership practice rather than an annual planning event.

Engagement driver analysis linked to business outcomes
Agreed leadership priorities and behavioral commitments
Communication cascade plan and manager discussion guides
Pulse survey design focused on predictive engagement drivers
Leadership operating rhythm and engagement dashboard

Customers and patients experience more consistent service when functions pull in the same direction. faqs.q: What does leadership alignment actually mean?
faqs.a: Leadership alignment means senior leaders share an understanding of the organization's priorities, agree on the tradeoffs involved, and behave and communicate consistently with those choices. It does not mean everyone agrees on everything. Healthy teams debate vigorously, then commit. Alignment becomes visible when employees in different functions describe the same priorities and see leaders making decisions that reflect them.

faqs.q: How does leadership alignment affect employee engagement?
faqs.a: Engagement depends heavily on clarity, trust in leadership decisions and a sense that one's work matters. Misaligned leaders undermine all three, because employees receive conflicting priorities and see resources contradict words. When leaders align and act consistently, the conditions for engagement improve. We measure the specific drivers that matter in your organization so leaders can see that connection in their own data.

faqs.q: We already run an annual engagement survey. What would you add?
faqs.a: We analyze your existing data to identify which drivers actually predict retention, performance or other outcomes you care about, instead of treating every item equally. We then connect those drivers to leadership behaviors and design shorter, more frequent pulse measures to track them. This turns the survey from an annual report card into a set of leading indicators leaders can act on.

faqs.q: How long does an alignment engagement take?
faqs.a: The initial diagnostic and alignment sessions typically take eight to twelve weeks. Many clients then continue with quarterly reviews and pulse measurement over the following year, which helps alignment survive changes in market conditions and leadership. The timing depends on the size of the leadership group and how much change the organization is navigating.

services.name: Behavioral Change Management
services.meta_description: Behavioral change management that treats transformation as specific behaviors to design, test and measure, rather than announcements and training alone.
services.summary: Change management grounded in behavioral science: define the behaviors change requires, remove barriers, design prompts and measure adoption as it happens.
services.lede: Behavioral change management treats every transformation as a set of specific behaviors that people must start, stop or do differently. We identify those behaviors, diagnose what blocks them, design interventions and measure adoption in real time.
challenge: Most change programs rely on communication and training. Leaders announce the new system, process or structure, people attend sessions, and the organization assumes behavior will follow. Often it does not. Employees revert to familiar workarounds, adoption stalls at the enthusiasts, and the business case quietly erodes. The problem is not resistance in the abstract. It is that the new behavior is harder, less rewarding or less prompted than the old one, and nobody designed for that.

Change efforts also tend to measure activity rather than behavior: emails sent, sessions delivered, licenses provisioned. These measures say little about whether people are actually working differently. By the time lagging outcomes reveal the problem, momentum is lost and skepticism has grown. Behavioral change management starts from the behaviors themselves, uses established models to understand barriers, and tracks early signals of adoption so leaders can intervene while there is still time.

approach.title: Specify the target behaviors
approach.body: We work with leaders to translate the change into concrete behaviors for each affected group: who needs to do what, when and how often. Contextual interviews and observation reveal the current workflow, the workarounds people rely on and the informal leaders who shape how colleagues respond. This replaces vague goals with a clear picture of what must change.

approach.title: Diagnose barriers and adoption signals
approach.body: Using the COM-B model, we assess whether each behavior is blocked by capability, opportunity or motivation. We analyze system logs, workflow data and surveys to find early adoption signals and behavioral segments, from early adopters to quiet holdouts. These become predictive KPIs that show whether change is taking hold long before final outcomes arrive.

approach.title: Design for the barrier
approach.body: We design interventions matched to each barrier: simplifying steps and removing friction where ability is the issue, adjusting incentives, recognition and social proof where motivation is weak, and adding timely prompts in the flow of work. Leaders and managers receive coaching on the behaviors they must model, since people watch what leaders do more closely than what they say.

approach.title: Pilot before broad rollout
approach.body: We test interventions with pilot groups, comparing adoption signals against similar groups where possible. Short feedback cycles show which prompts, supports and messages actually change behavior. We refine the approach before full rollout, reducing the risk of scaling a change plan that looks reasonable on paper but fails in practice.

approach.title: Sustain the new behaviors
approach.body: We support rollout across the organization, equip managers with dashboards that track adoption signals, and coach leaders to reinforce new habits. Change agents and peer networks help spread practices. We plan for the predictable dip after launch, so that support continues until the new behaviors are routine and the old ways are no longer easier.

COM-B barrier diagnosis and behavioral segmentation

services.impact_lens: Poorly managed change is exhausting for employees, who absorb the confusion, extra workload and repeated reversals. Behavioral change management respects people by making new ways of working genuinely easier and by listening to the barriers they face. When change succeeds, customers and patients benefit from improved processes and technology. In public-facing and health organizations, successful adoption of better practices can directly improve service, safety and access for the communities they serve.

faqs.q: How is behavioral change management different from traditional change management?
faqs.a: Traditional change management often focuses on stakeholder communication, training and readiness assessments. Behavioral change management keeps those elements but starts from specific behaviors and uses behavioral science to understand why people do or do not adopt them. It designs interventions for the actual barriers, tests them in pilots, and measures adoption through behavioral signals rather than activity counts.

faqs.q: What is the COM-B model?
faqs.a: COM-B is a behavior change framework that holds that behavior depends on capability, opportunity and motivation. Capability includes knowledge and skills. Opportunity includes physical and social factors in the environment. Motivation includes both reflective intentions and automatic habits and emotions. Diagnosing which component is weak for a given behavior helps us select interventions that fit, instead of defaulting to more training.

faqs.q: How do you measure adoption during a change?
faqs.a: We define leading indicators tied to the target behaviors, such as frequency of use of a new feature, completion of a new process step, or quality of handoffs. These often come from system logs and workflow data, supplemented by short pulse surveys. Segmenting by behavior shows who has adopted, who is struggling and who has not started, so support can be targeted.

faqs.q: Does this approach work for technology implementations?
faqs.a: Yes, technology adoption is one of the most common applications. New systems usually change many small daily behaviors, and adoption often fails because the new tool adds steps or disrupts familiar routines. We combine behavioral change management with usability insight to reduce friction, design prompts in the workflow and give managers clear signals about adoption progress.

services.name: High-Performance Culture Design
services.meta_description: High-performance culture design that turns values into observable behaviors, routines and systems, so culture becomes a measurable driver of performance.
services.summary: Culture design that translates values into everyday behaviors, rituals and systems, then measures whether the culture you want is actually emerging.
services.lede: A high-performance culture is the sum of behaviors people repeat because the organization makes them easy, expected and rewarded. We help leaders define those behaviors, design the systems that reinforce them and measure whether culture is moving.
challenge: Most organizations can recite their values, but few can say what those values look like on an ordinary Tuesday. Statements such as integrity, customer focus or ownership are open to interpretation, so each team quietly develops its own version. Meanwhile, the real culture is shaped by what gets promoted, funded, tolerated and celebrated. When those signals contradict the stated values, employees learn quickly which ones really count, and cynicism soon follows.

Culture work is often treated as a branding exercise or an offsite activity, disconnected from the systems that shape daily behavior: hiring criteria, performance reviews, meeting practices, decision processes and recognition. A high-performance culture cannot be declared. It must be designed into those systems and modeled by leaders, then measured over time. Without that, culture initiatives produce posters and slogans, while the behaviors that drive performance and wellbeing stay the same.

approach.title: Understand the culture as lived
approach.body: We conduct interviews, focus groups and observation across levels and locations, and review artifacts such as performance criteria, promotion decisions and meeting practices. We ask employees to describe the behaviors that actually get rewarded and the ones that get people in trouble. This reveals the gap between stated values and lived culture, with concrete examples.

approach.title: Measure culture as behavior
approach.body: We design culture measures rooted in observable behaviors rather than abstract sentiment, using psychometrically sound survey items, network patterns and operational data where available. We identify which cultural behaviors predict outcomes such as retention, quality or customer satisfaction, so leaders know which aspects of culture most deserve investment.

approach.title: Translate values into behaviors and systems
approach.body: With leaders and employee representatives, we define each value as a few specific behaviors, including what it looks like at different levels. We then redesign the systems that shape those behaviors: hiring questions, onboarding, recognition, performance conversations, meeting norms and decision rights. Leaders commit to visible role-modeling, which matters more than any written statement.

approach.title: Pilot culture interventions
approach.body: We pilot new rituals, recognition practices or performance approaches in selected teams and compare behavioral measures with other groups. Employee feedback shows whether changes feel authentic or performative. Testing helps the organization avoid broad culture launches that look impressive but generate cynicism when daily experience does not match the message.

approach.title: Embed and sustain
approach.body: We help leaders roll successful practices across the organization, build culture into leadership development and onboarding, and track culture indicators on a regular dashboard. We coach senior leaders on consistency, since a single high-profile exception can undo months of work. Culture becomes something managed with the same discipline as any other performance driver.

services.impact_lens: Culture shapes whether people feel respected, safe to raise concerns and able to do meaningful work. A well-designed high-performance culture supports both results and wellbeing, rather than trading one for the other. Customers and patients feel culture directly in how they are treated. Cultures that reward candor and learning also tend to catch ethical and safety problems earlier, protecting the communities an organization serves and the integrity of its mission.

faqs.q: Can culture really be designed?
faqs.a: Culture cannot be dictated, but it can be shaped deliberately. Culture emerges from repeated behaviors, and behaviors respond to what is easy, expected, modeled and rewarded. By designing the systems around people, including hiring, recognition, decision processes and leadership example, organizations can make desired behaviors more likely. Measurement then shows whether the culture is actually moving in the intended direction.

faqs.q: What makes a culture high-performance?
faqs.a: A high-performance culture combines high standards with high support. People know what excellent work looks like, hold each other accountable, speak up about problems and learn from mistakes. Psychological safety and accountability reinforce each other rather than compete. The specific behaviors vary by organization and strategy, which is why we define them through research rather than adopting a generic list.

faqs.q: How do you measure culture?
faqs.a: We measure culture through observable behaviors rather than general sentiment. Survey items describe specific actions, such as whether colleagues raise concerns in meetings or share credit, and are tested for reliability. Where possible we add operational signals and qualitative evidence. We also analyze which cultural behaviors predict outcomes such as retention or quality, so leaders focus on what matters most.

faqs.q: How long does culture change take?
faqs.a: Meaningful culture change usually unfolds over one to three years, although early shifts in specific behaviors can appear within months when systems and leadership behavior change together. We structure engagements in phases, with a diagnostic and design period followed by pilots and staged rollout, and regular measurement so leaders can see progress and adjust.

services.name: Leadership for High-Growth Companies
services.meta_description: Coaching for founders and leadership teams in high-growth companies: delegation, structure, hiring and decision rights that scale as the organization grows.
services.summary: Coaching and advisory for founders and leadership teams navigating rapid growth, from first managers to a professional executive team.
services.lede: Leadership for high-growth companies requires leaders to reinvent their roles every time the organization doubles. We coach founders and executive teams through those transitions, building the delegation, structure and team habits that let growth continue.
challenge: In a fast-growing company, the behaviors that created early success often become constraints. Founders who made every decision now slow the organization. Informal communication that worked for a small team fails as new people join. Early employees promoted into leadership roles struggle to manage teams they once worked alongside. The organization outgrows its leadership habits faster than anyone can adapt, and the symptoms appear as missed targets, burnout and the departure of valued people.

Growth also brings investors, boards and new executives with different expectations. Founders must learn to lead through others, build a leadership team they trust, and let go of work they love without losing the culture and product insight that made the company distinctive. These transitions are predictable, but each feels new to the people living through it. Leadership for high-growth companies requires preparing for the next stage before the current one breaks.

approach.title: Read the growth stage
approach.body: We interview founders, executives, board members and a cross-section of employees, and review organizational structure, decision flow and hiring plans. We identify where the company sits on its growth path and which leadership habits are already becoming bottlenecks. Founders often recognize the problems but have not seen how they connect.

approach.title: Spot the early warnings
approach.body: We look for signals that leadership capacity is falling behind growth: decision queues around one person, rising cycle times, regretted attrition, engagement dips in specific teams, or customer issues that cross functional boundaries. These leading indicators help leaders anticipate problems instead of reacting after a key person leaves or a critical launch slips.

approach.title: Design the next-stage leadership model
approach.body: We help founders and executives define their evolving roles, clarify decision rights and design the structure, rhythm and leadership layers the next stage requires. This includes hiring profiles for key roles, onboarding plans for new executives and individual coaching plans for leaders whose roles are changing faster than their habits.

approach.title: Try the new model in practice
approach.body: We help leaders experiment with delegation, new meeting structures and decision processes over defined periods, then review together what actually happened. Pulse feedback from teams shows whether changes are reducing friction or simply moving it. Adjustments are made quickly, matching the pace of a fast-growing organization.

approach.title: Grow leaders ahead of the curve
approach.body: We build leadership capability in the layers below the executive team through team coaching, first-time manager development and shared management practices. Founders receive continuing coaching as their roles evolve. The goal is an organization where leadership capacity grows slightly ahead of the business rather than perpetually trailing it.

faqs.q: When should a founder start working with a leadership coach?
faqs.a: Ideally before a major transition rather than after a crisis. Good moments include right after a significant funding round, when hiring the first senior executives, or when the founder notices they have become the bottleneck for decisions. Early coaching helps founders anticipate predictable challenges, but coaching is also valuable mid-transition, when the pressure is most visible.

faqs.q: How do you help founders learn to delegate?
faqs.a: We treat delegation as a set of behaviors, not a personality trait. Founders identify which decisions and tasks to hand off, define clear outcomes and boundaries, choose appropriate check-in points and resist the urge to take work back. We use small experiments, starting with lower-risk decisions, and gather feedback from the people receiving the delegated work to refine the approach.

faqs.q: Do you work with boards and investors?
faqs.a: Yes, with the leader's knowledge and agreement. Boards and investors are important stakeholders in a growing company's leadership development, and their perspective often helps clarify expectations. We contract carefully so that confidentiality is respected, and we can support conversations between founders and boards about leadership roles, succession and executive hiring.

faqs.q: How is this different from general executive coaching?
faqs.a: It includes executive coaching, but it also addresses the organizational design questions that growth raises: structure, decision rights, leadership layers and executive hiring. We focus on the specific transitions high-growth companies face and draw on direct experience founding and building companies. The work typically spans the founder, the executive team and the next layer of managers.

services.name: Health Behavior Change Design
services.meta_title: Health Behavior Change Design and Consulting
services.meta_description: Health behavior change design grounded in behavioral medicine: COM-B diagnosis, motivational design and testing for programs that help people stay healthier.
services.summary: Evidence-based health behavior change design for programs, products and services that help people start and sustain healthier routines.
services.lede: We apply behavioral medicine and design to health behavior change, helping organizations build programs and products that make healthy actions easier to start, more rewarding to repeat and more likely to last.
challenge: Most people already know they should move more, sleep better, take their medications or attend screenings. The gap is not information; it is translating intention into consistent action amid busy lives, competing priorities, cost, stress and habit. Yet many health programs still rely primarily on education and reminders, assuming that knowledge will produce behavior. When participation drops, the response is often more messages, which people quickly and understandably learn to ignore.

Health behavior change is also highly individual and contextual. A person managing diabetes while working night shifts faces different barriers than a retiree with limited mobility or a young parent with little time. Programs designed for an imagined average participant miss most real ones. Without careful diagnosis, segmentation by behavior and testing, organizations invest in interventions that look sensible but fail to move the behaviors that actually influence health outcomes.

approach.title: Understand behavior in context
approach.body: We interview participants, caregivers and frontline staff, and observe where the target behavior does or does not happen. Contextual inquiry and journey mapping reveal real barriers: confusing instructions, time conflicts, costs, side effects, low confidence or competing demands. We pay attention to health literacy and cultural context, which often explain more than motivation alone.

approach.title: Find the behaviors that predict outcomes
approach.body: We analyze program, claims, app or clinical data to identify the specific behaviors and early moments that predict longer-term engagement and health outcomes. We look for behavioral types, such as people who start strong then fade, and the conversion points where participants commit or drop out. These become predictive KPIs for the program.

approach.title: Match interventions to barriers
approach.body: Using COM-B, the Fogg Behavior Model and self-determination theory, we design interventions matched to each barrier: simpler first steps, well-timed prompts, implementation intentions, social support, feedback and motivational interviewing techniques that strengthen a person's own reasons for change. We respect autonomy throughout, avoiding pressure tactics that undermine long-term motivation.

approach.title: Pilot and compare
approach.body: We test interventions through pilots, A/B tests or staged rollouts, measuring both immediate behaviors and longer-term engagement. Where clinical outcomes are relevant, we work with clinical partners to design appropriate evaluation. Usability testing ensures that materials and tools are understandable to participants with varied health literacy and abilities.

approach.title: Implement and sustain
approach.body: We help teams roll out successful interventions, train staff in behavior change techniques such as motivational interviewing, and build dashboards that track predictive KPIs. We plan for maintenance as well as initiation, since many health behaviors fade after initial enthusiasm, and we design supports that help participants recover after lapses rather than giving up.

Participant journey map with barriers and conversion points

services.impact_lens: Health behavior change is one of the most direct ways behavioral science serves the social good. faqs.q: What models of health behavior change do you use?
faqs.a: We draw on several established frameworks, choosing based on the problem. COM-B helps diagnose whether capability, opportunity or motivation is the main barrier. The Fogg Behavior Model highlights the role of ability and prompts. Self-determination theory guides how to support lasting motivation through autonomy, competence and connection. Motivational interviewing informs conversations that strengthen people's own reasons for change.

faqs.q: Why do health programs that rely on education often fail?
faqs.a: Most people already know what they should do. Information addresses capability, but behavior also depends on opportunity, such as time, access and cost, and on motivation, including habits and emotions. Education alone rarely changes these. Effective health behavior change design identifies the specific barriers for specific groups and designs interventions that make the healthy behavior easier, more prompted and more rewarding.

faqs.q: How do you make sure behavior change design is ethical?
faqs.a: We design to help people do what they already want to do for their own health. That means transparency, respect for autonomy, avoiding fear-based or shaming messages, and protecting privacy in data use. We test materials with participants, including people with limited health literacy, and we decline approaches that exploit vulnerability. Ethical persuasion tends to produce more durable behavior change as well.

faqs.q: Can you help us evaluate an existing health program?
faqs.a: Yes. We often start with an existing program, analyzing participation data, interviewing participants and staff, and mapping where people drop out. This diagnosis usually reveals a few points where targeted redesign can improve engagement. We then help design and test changes, rather than rebuilding the program from scratch, and we define the measures that will show whether those changes are working.

services.name: Patient Engagement & Medication Adherence
services.meta_title: Patient Engagement and Medication Adherence Design
services.meta_description: Behavioral design for patient engagement and medication adherence: diagnose adherence barriers, segment patients by behavior and test interventions that help.
services.summary: Behavioral science for patient engagement and medication adherence, from diagnosing adherence barriers to designing and testing interventions with real patients.
services.lede: Improving medication adherence and patient engagement starts with understanding why patients do not take medications or attend follow-up as planned. We diagnose the real barriers and design interventions that help patients follow treatment plans they agree with.
challenge: Nonadherence is rarely a single problem. Some patients forget. Others intentionally skip doses because of side effects, cost, doubts about benefit or fear of dependence. Some never fill the first prescription. Others stop when they feel better, or when symptoms they expected never appear. Complex regimens, low health literacy, depression, cognitive difficulties and limited support at home all play a role. Treating these different patterns with the same reminder program helps some patients and frustrates many others.

Organizations also struggle to see adherence clearly. Pharmacy refill data, claims, device data and clinical notes sit in different systems, so the early signals of disengagement, such as a late refill or a missed appointment, are noticed too late. Engagement programs often measure enrollment or message opens rather than whether patients actually take medication or follow up. Without integrated data and behavioral insight, it is difficult to know which patients need what kind of support and when.

approach.title: Listen to patients and care teams
approach.body: We interview patients, caregivers, pharmacists, nurses and physicians, and observe how treatment plans are explained and experienced. We pay close attention to unintentional barriers, such as forgetting and complexity, and intentional ones, such as beliefs about medication, side effects and cost. Patients are treated as experts in their own lives.

approach.title: Integrate data and find early signals
approach.body: We bring together refill, claims, appointment, app and clinical data where available to identify early predictors of disengagement and distinct adherence types, from first-fill abandonment to gradual drift. These patterns become predictive KPIs that let care teams intervene before nonadherence affects health outcomes, rather than discovering it months later.

approach.title: Design support for each barrier
approach.body: We design interventions matched to adherence types: regimen simplification and habit anchoring for forgetting, motivational interviewing conversations for ambivalence, cost navigation for financial barriers, and plain-language education for misunderstanding. Messages, outreach timing and channels are tailored, and care team workflows are designed so support is realistic within existing staff capacity.

approach.title: Pilot with real patients
approach.body: We test interventions with patient groups through pilots or randomized comparisons, measuring refill behavior, follow-up attendance and patient experience. Usability testing with patients of varied ages, abilities and literacy levels ensures that tools and materials work in practice. We collaborate with clinical and compliance teams to ensure tests are appropriate and safe.

approach.title: Operationalize adherence support
approach.body: We help organizations embed successful interventions into care team workflows, pharmacy programs or digital products, train staff in brief motivational techniques and build dashboards that flag patients at risk. We design for sustainability, so support continues reliably after launch, and we establish regular reviews to refine the program as patient populations change.

faqs.q: What are the most common barriers to medication adherence?
faqs.a: Barriers are often grouped into unintentional and intentional types. Unintentional barriers include forgetting, complex dosing schedules, cognitive difficulties and disrupted routines. Intentional barriers involve choices shaped by side effects, cost, doubts about benefit, worries about dependence or feeling well. Health literacy, depression, social support and access to pharmacies also matter. Effective programs identify which barriers apply to which patients.

faqs.q: How does motivational interviewing help with adherence?
faqs.a: Motivational interviewing is a collaborative conversation style that helps people explore their own ambivalence and strengthen their own reasons for change. For patients uncertain about a medication, it avoids arguing or lecturing, which can increase resistance. Clinicians and pharmacists can learn brief techniques that fit into short encounters. We train care teams and design conversation guides grounded in this approach.

faqs.q: Do reminders and apps improve medication adherence?
faqs.a: Reminders can help patients whose main barrier is forgetting, especially when tied to existing routines. They do little for patients who have intentional reasons for not taking medication, such as side effects or cost. Apps often show strong initial use that fades. We help organizations target digital tools to the patients they actually help and combine them with human support where needed.

faqs.q: How do you handle patient data privacy?
faqs.a: We work within our clients' privacy, security and compliance frameworks, including applicable health privacy regulations, and follow data minimization principles. Analysis typically uses de-identified or limited data sets under appropriate agreements. We also consider privacy from the patient's perspective when designing outreach, avoiding messages that could reveal sensitive health information to others.

services.name: Digital Health Product Design

services.summary: Behavioral and experience design for digital health products, focused on sustained engagement, usability for real patients and evidence of behavior change.
services.lede: Our digital health product design work combines behavioral medicine, human-computer interaction and engagement analytics to help teams build apps, platforms and connected tools that patients and clinicians adopt, understand and keep using.
challenge: Digital health products face a familiar pattern: strong downloads, enthusiastic early use, then steep decline. Many apps are designed for motivated, tech-savvy users, while the people who need them most may be older, unwell, fatigued, managing multiple conditions or uneasy with technology. Features multiply in an attempt to engage everyone, increasing complexity and burden. Meanwhile, clinicians are asked to recommend tools they have little time to understand and that may add work to already crowded days.

Digital health teams also struggle to connect engagement metrics with outcomes. Daily active users and session length say little about whether a product is changing health behavior. Investors, payers and health system partners increasingly expect evidence of meaningful engagement and outcomes. Without a behavioral model of how the product should create change, teams optimize for activity that may not matter and miss the moments that predict whether a user will stay and benefit.

approach.title: Research with patients and clinicians
approach.body: We conduct contextual research with patients, caregivers and clinicians, observing how they manage health in daily life and where a digital tool could genuinely help. Drawing on our experience building software for people with chronic illness, we pay attention to fatigue, cognitive load, accessibility, privacy concerns and how products fit into clinical workflows.

approach.title: Build the engagement model
approach.body: We analyze product analytics to identify the early behaviors and activation moments that predict sustained use and the behavioral types of users, such as steady trackers or crisis-driven users. We define predictive engagement KPIs linked to the product's theory of change, separating meaningful engagement from activity that merely inflates usage numbers.

approach.title: Design for behavior and usability
approach.body: We apply behavioral design, persuasive technology principles and HCI to onboarding, core flows, notifications and feedback. Typical work includes reducing the effort of key actions, designing prompts that fit real routines, presenting data patients can interpret and act on, and supporting autonomy and competence rather than relying on streaks and points alone.

approach.title: Usability and experiments
approach.body: We run usability testing with representative users, including people with limited health or digital literacy, and design A/B tests and pilots to measure the effect of changes on predictive KPIs. Where products make clinical claims, we coordinate with clinical and regulatory teams to plan appropriate evaluation.

approach.title: Grow with evidence
approach.body: We help product teams build an experimentation practice, engagement dashboards and research routines so they can keep improving after our work ends. We support evidence planning for payer and health system conversations, and advise on scaling to new populations without losing the usability and behavioral fit that made the product work.
